parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically: with α=5 (strong right skew), the mean ≈ ξ + ω·δ·√(2/π) where δ=α/√(1+α²)=0.981, giving mean≈1.75; mode≈1.5; central 95% mass ≈ [0.2, 3.6], close to the stated interval.

strategies.rationale: Public EP and WP models consistently show NFL coaches are far too conservative here; the field-position cost of failing is lower than assumed, and the expected-points gain of converting is substantial.
strategies.recommendation: Go for it on 4th-and-short (≤4 yards) anywhere between your own 40 and the opponent's 35 in any game script within roughly 14 points. Expand to 4th-and-medium (5–7) in plus territory when trailing.
strategies.title: Aggressive 4th-Down Conversion in Opponent Territory

strategies.rationale: Expected-points models show passes outperform runs on 1st and 2nd down in most neutral situations; the run bias persists from outdated risk aversion rather than EV evidence.
strategies.recommendation: Increase first-down pass rate from the league-average ~55% toward 65–70% in the first and second quarters when the score is within one score, accepting slightly higher negative-play variance.
strategies.title: Pass-Heavier on Early Downs in Neutral Scripts

strategies.rationale: Research on drive survival and explosive plays shows that preventing 20+ yard gains raises defensive success rate more than marginal run-defense gains cost; offenses struggle with consistency over 10+ play drives.
strategies.recommendation: Default to two-deep safety looks (Cover-2/6) on 1st and 2nd-and-long, trading run-defense efficiency for explosive-pass prevention and forcing offenses to sustain long drives.
strategies.title: Two-Deep Safety Shell as Base Coverage on Early Downs

distribution_family.justification: The effect is small and roughly symmetric — it helps in a narrow window and rarely costs much, but could backfire if the penalty flips field position in a closer-than-assumed case.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Standard kneel sequences sometimes leave too much clock; a 5-yard penalty that costs no practical field position can remove 8–12 seconds the opponent needs. Analytics is silent because the scenario is too specific for public models.
strategies.recommendation: When leading by 1–8 points with under 3:00 remaining and the opponent has all timeouts, intentionally incur delay-of-game penalties before kneel-downs on 3rd/4th down to burn additional seconds without losing field position that matters.
strategies.title: Strategic Delay-of-Game to Compress Opponent Possessions Late

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value 0.3 lies inside [−1.5, 2.0]; student_t support is all reals.

distribution_family.justification: Symmetric belief with genuinely heavy tails: tempo could produce a large positive effect if defenses fatigue, or a large negative effect if it produces quick three-and-outs that expose your own defense.
distribution_family.name: student_t

strategies.rationale: Public analytics are mixed — tempo correlates with both explosive plays and three-and-outs. My intuition is that the communication and substitution stress on defenses is undervalued and creates favorable personnel mismatches the models don't capture.
strategies.recommendation: Run no-huddle tempo as the default offensive mode for the first three drives of each half, substituting pace for pre-snap motion complexity and forcing defenses to play base personnel.
strategies.title: No-Huddle Up-Tempo as Base Offense, Not Just Situational

distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically with α=−3 (left skew): δ=−0.949; mean≈ξ+ω·(−0.756)≈0.5−0.756=−0.26; mode≈0.1; central 95% ≈ [−1.1, 0.8], close to stated interval.

strategies.rationale: Conventional defenses fight for a field-goal stop, but mathematically a touchdown against you is often nearly equivalent to a field goal when you need two scores, and forcing the clock to run is the bigger enemy. Analytics is silent on this specific trade-off in public literature.
strategies.recommendation: When trailing by 9–16 points with under 5:00 remaining and the opponent is in the red zone, deliberately permit a touchdown (soft coverage, no resistance) rather than forcing a field goal, to preserve clock and maximize your remaining possessions.
strategies.title: Deliberately Allow Quick Scores When Trailing by 2+ Scores Late
